main_damage_causes: Omission of Lupin's explicit self-condemnation for cowardice in the Shrieking Shack — the moral core of his character arc is never spoken aloud
Collapse of the gradual mentor-relationship building (office visit, tea scene, Snape's potion delivery) into a single front-loaded bridge monologue, reducing the texture of the Lupin-Harry bond
Lupin's agency and moral reasoning in the Shrieking Shack are subordinated to Sirius Black, making him a follower rather than the scene's voice of reason and due process

Collapse of Lupin's intellectual and mediating authority in the Grimmauld Place briefing, redistributing his agency to Sirius and Moody and leaving him as a functional background presence rather than a primary adult voice

Loss of emotional depth in the post-Sirius-death restraint scene, which in the book is the central evidence of Lupin's own grief and his bond with the Marauders, reducing a relationship beat to a plot function

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Bridge walk) — Lupin shares memories of Lily unprompted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes no scene where Lupin volunteers personal memories of Lily to Harry on the bridge. Their one-on-one conversations are initiated by Harry's questions (about the boggart, the dementors) and Lupin is warm but measured, never delivering an extended emotional monologue about Lily. His connection to James and Lily is revealed gradually, organically, and culminates in the Shrieking Shack.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin delivers an unsolicited, lyrical speech about Lily: 'She was not only a singularly gifted witch but an uncommonly kind woman. She had a way of seeing the beauty in whoever she met...' He volunteers intimate emotional content about both Lily and James ('James had, shall we say, a certain talent for trouble') in a way that skips the gradual revelation the book structures carefully across the year.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully parcels out Lupin's connection to Harry's parents — it is a slow discovery that pays off emotionally in the Shrieking Shack and farewell scene. The film front-loads this intimacy, collapsing the gradual trust-building and making Lupin's later revelations feel redundant rather than revelatory. It also makes Lupin slightly sentimental and expansive where the book keeps him private and restrained, changing his characterization from quietly wounded to openly elegiac.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Bridge walk) — Lupin's self-deprecating humor about Hogsmeade
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has no corresponding bridge scene. Lupin's humor in the book is dry and understated — 'I haven't poisoned that chocolate, you know' — always brief, never a set piece. His wit emerges incidentally within other business.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin opens the bridge conversation with a comic routine: 'Well, don't feel too bad. I was roundly disappointed the first time I went. No. I was just trying to make you feel better. Honeydukes' sweets are the best in the world...' This is a multi-line joke with a deliberate punchline structure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor tonal shift. The joke is not out of character in spirit but the delivery is more performative than the book's version of Lupin, who tends to let wit emerge as a side effect rather than leading with it. Low damage in isolation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Boggart lesson) — Lupin steps in front of Harry during the boggart exercise with no prior explanation and no post-class conversation establishing the reason
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book splits this into two beats: (1) Lupin visibly redirects the boggart away from Harry during the lesson, (2) Harry later visits Lupin's office specifically to ask why, and Lupin explains he feared it would become Voldemort — then the conversation deepens into dementor discussion, Snape's potion delivery, and Harry's nascent trust. The office visit is a key relationship-building scene establishing Lupin as someone Harry can confide in.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin steps in front of Harry when the boggart turns to a Dementor, dispatching it himself. There is a brief private glance between them as students exit, but the follow-up office conversation — with its tea, the grindylow, Snape's potion, and Lupin's frank explanation — is entirely absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The office scene is where Lupin and Harry's mentor relationship is cemented in private. Lupin explains his reasoning (feared Voldemort), Harry reveals he thought of dementors instead, Lupin responds with genuine admiration ('That suggests what you fear most is fear — very wise'). This exchange establishes mutual respect and opens the door to the Patronus lessons. Its absence means the film's Lupin-Harry bond is built almost entirely on the bridge scene and Patronus training, reducing the texture of their relationship. The grindylow, the tea, Snape's potion delivery and Harry's suspicion of Snape — all absent — further thin Lupin's characterization as a warm, curious, slightly eccentric presence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13/14 (Corridor/Lupin's office — Marauder's Map confrontation) — Lupin does not acknowledge being a Marauder and gives a harsher, more parental lecture
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Lupin takes the map from Harry after the Snape confrontation, he steps outside, lowers his voice, expresses astonishment that Harry didn't hand it in, and then cryptically explains that 'these mapmakers would have wanted to lure you out of school — they'd think it extremely entertaining,' followed by Harry asking 'Do you know them?' Lupin walks away without answering directly — a tantalizing evasion that the reader understands in retrospect. The scene is playful even in its seriousness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin delivers a stern lecture framed around James and Lily's sacrifice: 'Your father didn't set much store by rules either. But he and your mother did give their lives to save yours. Gambling their sacrifice...' He then reacts to Harry's mention of Pettigrew on the map with only a half-second hesitation before dismissing it. The connection to the Marauders is not teased; instead the scene becomes a moral lecture invoking Harry's dead parents as emotional leverage.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this scene is carefully layered — Lupin's evasiveness about the mapmakers is a subtle signal to attentive readers and a character beat showing his complicated relationship with his own past. The film replaces this with a straightforward parental reprimand that invokes James and Lily, which makes Lupin feel more like an authority figure than a man with a private, complex history. It loses the delicious irony of Lupin scolding Harry for the map he helped create.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Shrieking Shack) — Lupin immediately embraces Black before any explanation, then agrees to kill Pettigrew with minimal resistance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin disarms all three children first, then speaks in a 'very tense voice' asking 'Where is he, Sirius?' — he approaches the situation as an investigator, needing to confirm his reading of the map before acting. He restrains Black physically when Black lunges at Pettigrew ('Sirius, NO! Lupin yelled, launching himself forward'). He insists 'They've got a right to know everything!' He gives a lengthy explanation of the Marauder backstory. When he and Black agree to kill Pettigrew, Harry intervenes and Lupin immediately defers: 'Very well. Stand aside, Harry.' His moral position is that of a man who believes execution is deserved but yields to Harry's moral authority without much struggle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin enters, says 'Looking a bit ragged, aren't we, Sirius?' — a taunting line — then almost immediately embraces Black. When Black says 'He dies. Now,' Lupin says 'Wait, Sirius—' but Black overrides him and Lupin nods: 'All right then. As you wish.' The extended backstory (Animagus transformation, Hogwarts years, Pettigrew's betrayal) is compressed and distributed differently, with Black doing more narrative work. The film skips Lupin's physical restraint of Black and his insistence on due process.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Lupin in this scene is the voice of reason holding chaos at bay — he physically stops Black, insists on explanation, and structures the revelation for the children. The film compresses this so that Lupin is more passive, essentially following Black's lead. The line 'All right then. As you wish' makes Lupin seem to capitulate to vigilante justice rather than being a man who, after exhaustive explanation, reaches the same conclusion and is then overridden by Harry. This weakens Lupin's moral agency in what is the climactic scene of his arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 15 (Shrieking Shack) — The full Marauder backstory and Lupin's self-accusation are not delivered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes extensive space to Lupin narrating the Marauder history: his werewolf bite as a child, Dumbledore's sympathy, the Shrieking Shack's construction, his friends becoming Animagi over three years, the near-misses while roaming, and crucially his self-condemnation: 'I sometimes felt guilty about betraying Dumbledore's trust... All this year I have been battling with myself, wondering whether I should tell Dumbledore that Sirius was an Animagus. But I didn't do it. Why? Because I was too cowardly.' This speech is Lupin's central act of moral reckoning — he names his own cowardice explicitly.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits the detailed Marauder origin story and, critically, omits Lupin's explicit self-accusation of cowardice. The backstory is condensed to bare plot essentials (Pettigrew betrayed the Potters, Scabbers is Pettigrew). Lupin's guilt and moral self-examination are not spoken.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's confession of cowardice is the emotional core of his arc. He is not simply a good man who was deceived — he is a good man who knew something, said nothing out of self-interest, and names that failing explicitly. This is what makes him a genuinely complex character rather than a victim of circumstance. Without it, his departure and resignation feel like misfortune happening to a passive figure rather than the consequence of a flawed man's long-running failure of nerve. This is the single most damaging omission to Lupin's characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (Lupin's farewell) — Lupin's resignation speech omits his acknowledgment of Dumbledore's trust and his werewolf stigma reflection; the Marauder's Map is returned with a wand flourish ('Mischief managed') rather than a verbal acknowledgment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin's farewell is quiet and somewhat broken. He explains Snape outed him, confirms parents will object, says 'I see their point. I could have bitten any of you... That must never happen again.' He returns both the Invisibility Cloak and the Marauder's Map with explicit acknowledgment: 'I am no longer your teacher, so I don't feel guilty about giving you back this as well.' He speaks about James: 'I have no hesitation in saying that James would have been highly disappointed if his son had never found any of the secret passages.' The scene is bittersweet and personal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin's farewell covers similar ground but adds the film-invented line 'people like me, well... let's just say I'm used to this by now,' which is slightly self-pitying rather than self-critical. He does not return the Invisibility Cloak (not a corpus-evidenced element in the film). He uses the map to perform 'Mischief managed' theatrically, then is simply gone. The scene ends on the Firebolt reveal rather than Harry's reflection on what he's lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film farewell is close to the book's but shifts slightly toward pathos ('I'm used to this') rather than the book's more dignified, self-aware sadness. The theatrical 'Mischief managed' flourish gives Lupin a showman's exit that fits the film's tone but softens the genuine loss of a mentor who is leaving because of his own failures as much as others' prejudice. Moderate damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 16 (Whomping Willow exterior) — Sirius Black delivers the 'you know the man you truly are, Remus' speech during transformation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has no equivalent scene. During the transformation, the text simply states: 'Lupin's face had gone rigid... his limbs began to shake.' There is no dialogue addressed to Lupin. Black shouts 'Run' and tries to intervene physically as a dog. Lupin's transformation is presented as sudden, horrifying, and beyond any appeal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Sirius wraps his arms around transforming Lupin and speaks: 'You know the man you truly are, Remus. This flesh is only flesh. This heart is where you truly live.' Lupin's wand drops in apparent response before Pettigrew grabs it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's transformation is frightening precisely because it is involuntary and total — no friendship or words can stop it, which is central to the tragedy of Lupin's condition. The film's version implies Sirius's appeal almost reaches Lupin, sentimentalizing the werewolf transformation and the Black-Lupin friendship in a way that slightly undercuts the horror of what Lupin is. It also re-centers the moment on Black rather than the terrifying loss of Lupin's agency. Moderate damage to the theme of werewolf stigma and involuntary transformation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place briefing, Lupin's single-line explanation of Fudge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus shows Lupin as a primary, authoritative voice in the Grimmauld Place debriefing: he explains the Ministry's denial, the Daily Prophet suppression, goblin politics, Voldemort's recruitment strategy, the need for Occlumency, and delivers nuanced political analysis across many exchanges (scenes 70, 78, 83, 88, 90, 92, 95, 97, 99, 102, 103, 108). He mediates between Sirius and Molly, advocates for Harry's right to information, and demonstrates strategic intelligence and moral clarity throughout.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film briefing scene, Lupin delivers a single explanatory speech: 'The Minister thinks Dumbledore's after his job... Fudge isn't in his right mind. It's been twisted and warped by fear...' This is his only substantive contribution. All other briefing content is handled by Sirius and Moody. Lupin's role as mediator, political analyst, and advocate for Harry is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book corpus establishes the Grimmauld Place briefing as one of Lupin's defining moments: he balances Sirius's recklessness, outmanoeuvres Molly's protectiveness, and demonstrates why Dumbledore trusts him. Reducing him to a single speech and transferring his agency to Sirius and Moody collapses his intellectual authority and his function as the adult the Order actually relies on for measured judgment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place briefing, Lupin absent from Sirius/Molly mediation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 78–84 show Lupin sharply intervening in the Sirius/Molly argument: 'Molly, you're not the only person at this table who cares about Harry' (to Molly), 'Sirius, sit down' (to Sirius), and 'I think Harry ought to be allowed a say in this.' He then physically leaves to silence Mrs. Black's portrait and returns to manage the room. This positions him as the group's calm authority, distinct from both Sirius's passion and Molly's anxiety.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Sirius/Molly argument (Film Scene 1) has no Lupin intervention. The argument plays out between Sirius, Molly, and Snape, with Lupin entirely silent. His line 'The Minister thinks Dumbledore's after his job' comes before this conflict, not as a mediating act within it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's mediation in the book is not incidental — it reveals his standing among the Order, his ability to check both Sirius and Molly, and his particular investment in Harry. Losing it flattens his relationship with both Sirius (where he is a brake, not just a companion) and with Harry (where he is an independent advocate, not just a bystander).

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place, Lupin's werewolf marginalisation and social vulnerability absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 102 has Lupin state with dry self-awareness: 'I'm not a very popular dinner guest with most of the community. It's an occupational hazard of being a werewolf.' Book scene 169 connects Umbridge's anti-werewolf legislation directly to Lupin's shabby appearance. These moments establish his social precarity as a lived, characterising reality.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no reference to Lupin's werewolf status in the context of his social standing, employment difficulties, or relationship with wizarding society's prejudice. Kreacher's line 'Mudblood and werewolves' (Film Scene 1) is the only acknowledgment of his condition, and it is hostile background noise, not characterisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's wry, dignified acknowledgment of his own marginalisation is a key character note — it shows resilience, self-knowledge, and the cost of his loyalty to Dumbledore's cause. Without it, his shabbiness reads as generic poverty rather than the consequence of systemic prejudice, and a thematic strand about discrimination within the wizarding world is severed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Department of Mysteries battle, Lupin's restraint of Harry after Sirius's death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 263–280 show Lupin physically restraining Harry for an extended, anguished sequence. Lupin's voice breaks ('He can't come back, because he's d—'), he struggles to contain Harry while clearly grief-stricken himself, drags him away from the archway, and the narration emphasises that every word costs him pain (scene 280). His own grief is present but subordinated to Harry's need — a sustained act of painful, selfless duty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2 shows Lupin grabbing Harry as Harry tries to follow Sirius through the veil, and Harry breaking free to chase Bellatrix. The physical restraint is present but brief. There is no audible break in Lupin's voice, no extended struggle, and no textual or visual signal that Lupin is simultaneously grieving his closest friend. The moment is functional rather than emotionally layered.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book corpus uses this scene to establish that Lupin's bond with Sirius is equal in depth to Harry's bond with his godfather — Lupin's breaking voice and the narrator's note that 'every word was causing him pain' are the primary evidence of their friendship's depth. The film reduces this to a physical plot beat, losing the emotional testimony to the Marauder relationship and diminishing the cost of Sirius's death to Lupin specifically.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place arrival, Lupin's welcoming presence and prefect backstory absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 6–31 show Lupin as the first person Harry recognises and trusts on arrival, the one who verifies Harry's identity via Patronus, manages the group's logistics, praises Harry's flying to Kingsley, and shepherds the whole operation with quiet competence. Book scenes 128–129 later establish the prefect anecdote — Lupin was the 'good boy' who 'failed dismally' to control James and Sirius — giving him self-deprecating wit and grounding his moral complexity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film arrival sequence (Film Scene 1) is led by Moody, with Tonks prominent. Lupin is present in the group but has no dialogue in the arrival or flight sequence. The prefect anecdote does not appear anywhere in the film corpus. Lupin's role as the trusted anchor of Harry's reintegration into the wizarding world is absorbed by Moody and Tonks.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's arrival sequence is the first extended portrait of adult-Lupin: competent, warm, quietly funny, Harry's primary point of trust. The prefect anecdote adds self-aware humour and reveals his complicated loyalty to James. Both are lost, leaving the film's Lupin without an establishing characterisation moment in the first act.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place, Lupin comforting Molly after Boggart absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 139–152 show Lupin walking in, instantly reading the situation (Mrs. Weasley's Boggart), dispelling it with a firm 'Riddikulus', comforting Molly on his shoulder, handing her a handkerchief, and then firmly but kindly reframing her fears: 'Molly, that's enough. This isn't like last time... And as for who's going to look after Ron and Ginny if you and Arthur died, what do you think we'd do, let them starve?' This is a full scene of emotional intelligence, practical reassurance, and paternal warmth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Boggart scene and Lupin's comfort of Molly Weasley do not appear in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is one of the clearest demonstrations of Lupin's emotional competence and his role as a sustaining figure for the Order's human core. Its absence removes a key beat showing him as someone others lean on — not just a tactician or a teacher — and weakens the audience's sense of why he is irreplaceable to this group.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place, Lupin's urgent Occlumency advocacy absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 194 and 246–251 show Lupin delivering a firm, private instruction to Harry about Occlumency ('Harry, I know you don't like Snape, but he is a superb Occlumens and we all — Sirius included — want you to learn to protect yourself') and later responding with alarm when he learns Snape has stopped the lessons ('Are you serious, Harry?... Harry there is nothing so important as you learning Occlumency! Do you understand me? Nothing!'). He physically restrains Sirius from storming up to Hogwarts and takes responsibility for addressing Snape himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No version of the Occlumency advocacy or the fireplace scene appears in the film corpus. Lupin's awareness of Voldemort's mental threat to Harry and his active intervention to protect Harry from it are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Occlumency is structurally central to Order of the Phoenix — its failure leads directly to Sirius's death. The book establishes Lupin as the adult who most urgently champions Harry learning it, and who tries to course-correct when it breaks down. Losing this removes Lupin's causal connection to the plot's central tragic chain and strips him of a major protective function.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Christmas party conversation about Snape/Draco
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin's rebuttal to Harry is measured, philosophically grounded, and personally revealing. He explains his nuanced view of Snape: 'I neither like nor dislike Severus... we shall never be bosom friends... But I do not forget that during the year I taught at Hogwarts, Severus made the Wolfsbane Potion for me every month, made it perfectly.' He also gently calls out Harry's inherited prejudice: 'You are determined to hate him, Harry... you have inherited an old prejudice.' The argument is reasoned, warm, and self-aware.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin cuts Harry off sharply with 'You're blinded by hatred' and then 'You are!' (marked 'sharply' in the script). The film reduces Lupin's nuanced, personally-grounded argument to a blunt, almost dismissive rebuke. The personal explanation about the Wolfsbane Potion — which humanizes both Lupin and his complicated relationship with Snape — is entirely absent. The film Lupin sounds more like a stressed authority figure shutting down debate than the thoughtful, self-reflective man of the books.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Lupin uses this moment to demonstrate emotional intelligence, personal honesty about his own biases, and a mature capacity to hold complexity. The film's sharp, dismissive tone strips away the introspective quality that defines book-Lupin's voice. It also removes the Wolfsbane detail, which is one of the rare moments where Lupin's relationship to his own condition and to Snape is illuminated with real specificity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Christmas party: Lupin's mission among werewolves entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book Christmas scene contains an extended, deeply characterizing conversation in which Lupin reveals he has been living undercover among werewolves for Dumbledore ('I've been living among my fellows, my equals... Nearly all of them are on Voldemort's side. Dumbledore wanted a spy and here I was... ready-made'). He speaks with bitter self-awareness, explains the difficulty of gaining their trust, introduces Greyback, and — crucially — reveals that Greyback was the one who bit him as a child. This is the primary scene establishing Lupin's arc, his relationship to his condition, and his personal history with Greyback.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Christmas scene contains no mention of Lupin's undercover mission, Greyback's identity, or Lupin's childhood backstory. The conversation is entirely redirected to Draco/Snape and then to the attack on the Burrow. None of this arc material appears elsewhere in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the defining arc passage for Lupin in HBP. His self-described role as 'ready-made' spy, his bitter acknowledgment of his own marginalization among werewolves, and the revelation about Greyback are central to understanding who he is and what he risks. Without it, Lupin's later relationship to Greyback (who attacks Bill), his emotional weight at the hospital wing, and the Tonks arc all lose grounding. The audience never understands that Lupin has been living in danger and self-sacrifice, which fundamentally changes how they read him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Christmas party: Half-Blood Prince conversation absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book contains a warm, characterizing exchange where Harry asks Lupin about the Half-Blood Prince, Lupin engages with gentle humor ('Is this a title you're thinking of adopting? I should have thought being the Chosen One would be enough'), and — crucially — confirms James was a pureblood who never asked to be called Prince. Lupin also reflects on Levicorpus being popular in his fifth year, and the conversation ends with the James-reminiscence that prompts Harry's excitement: 'Sometimes you remind me a lot of James. He called it my furry little problem in company.' This is one of the few warm, James-connected moments between Lupin and Harry in the book.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange is entirely absent from the film corpus. The Christmas scene moves from the Snape/Draco argument directly to the Burrow attack.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Half-Blood Prince conversation is one of the warmest Harry-Lupin interactions in HBP and one of the few moments where Lupin serves as a living connection to James. The 'furry little problem' line is also the sole moment of levity Lupin displays about his own condition in this book. Its absence weakens the Harry-Lupin relationship dynamic and removes a layer of Lupin's personality — his dry humor and his emotional tie to James — that does not appear elsewhere in the film corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Mr. Weasley's workshop: Lupin's character explained away by Arthur
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Lupin's sharpness and self-awareness through his own speech and behavior. He does not require external explanation or apology.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After the Christmas conversation, Arthur tells Harry privately: 'You'll have to forgive Remus. It takes its toll — his condition.' This frames Lupin's sharpness in the prior scene as a symptom of his lycanthropy rather than a considered, defensible position.
damaging_scenes.explanation: By having Arthur excuse Lupin's behavior as a byproduct of 'his condition,' the film inadvertently reduces Lupin's agency. In the book, Lupin's views on Snape are principled and deliberate, not emotionally compromised. This line pathologizes a character whose defining struggle is precisely the desire to be seen as more than his condition. It is a small moment but one that subtly undermines Lupin's intellectual authority.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 3-7 - Burrow attack: Lupin's role is reactive and peripheral
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Burrow attack does not occur in the books. However, within the film corpus, the book establishes Lupin as an active, capable participant in the Battle of the Astronomy Tower (fighting Death Eaters, providing tactical information, being a leader in the Order), and as someone with specific agency in dangerous situations.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: During the Burrow attack, Lupin's role is almost entirely reactive: he sniffs the air, his hand hairs rise, and he draws his wand to chase after Harry. The resolution of the confrontation with Greyback is achieved by Harry and Ginny together. Lupin arrives in the clearing after the fact with the rest of the group. Given that Greyback is the man who bit Lupin as a child — a fact just revealed in the book Christmas scene but absent from the film — Lupin has no notable interaction with Greyback at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a confrontation between Lupin and Greyback (implicitly, since both are present) but gives it to Harry and Ginny. Because the film has already omitted the revelation that Greyback bit Lupin, the missed opportunity is compounded: even if the audience knew the backstory, Lupin is sidelined. This transfers a moment of potential personal agency and dramatic resonance to other characters, and reduces Lupin to a supporting bystander in the scene where his personal nemesis appears.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film corpus overall: Lupin-Tonks relationship development absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book builds the Lupin-Tonks relationship across the whole volume through layered indirect evidence (Tonks's changed Patronus, her depression, her grey hair, Lupin trying to talk her round) culminating in the hospital wing scene where Tonks seizes Lupin's robes and declares 'I don't care!' and Lupin responds with his full self-deprecating refusal ('I am too old for you, too poor... too dangerous... Tonks deserves somebody young and whole'). This is one of the book's central emotional arcs and a key expression of Lupin's deepest flaw: his belief that he is unworthy of love.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no scene developing the Lupin-Tonks relationship. The only references are background staging: Tonks saying 'Sweetheart' to Lupin on the porch, and the stage direction noting they appear to be holding hands at Dumbledore's funeral. The hospital wing confrontation — the emotional climax of this arc — does not appear in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's refusal of love out of self-loathing ('I am too old, too poor, too dangerous') is his central character flaw in HBP and the emotional spine of his arc across the final two books. Without this scene, the audience has no understanding of why Lupin and Tonks are together in DH, no sense of what it cost either of them, and no framework for reading Lupin's later abandonment of Tonks during her pregnancy — itself a major moral failure the books set up here. This is the single most damaging omission in the film corpus: it removes a saga-level arc beat that redefines Lupin from tragic supporting figure to a man with a genuine, flawed inner life.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Sitting room/kitchen after Seven Potters, Lupin interrogates Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin 'grabbed Harry by the upper arm and dragged him, none too gently, back into the kitchen' — a firm but controlled action. He then asks the grindylow question with 'a small shake.' The physicality is present but measured, and Hagrid's protest ('Le' go of Harry!') and Lupin's explanation follow naturally in a private kitchen space.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Lupin grab 'a fistful of his shirt and hurl him against the wall' in front of the assembled group including Ginny, who shouts 'Remus! What're you doing!' The public spectacle and the heightened violence of the action make Lupin look unhinged rather than urgently cautious.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Lupin acts with terse, purposeful urgency — alarming but explicable. The film amplifies the physicality and makes it a public scene, which strips Lupin of the controlled professionalism that defines him and makes him seem temperamentally volatile rather than a man under extreme pressure exercising hard-headed security judgment.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Sitting room after Seven Potters, Lupin's explanation of the betrayal
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the grindylow question, the book gives Lupin a substantial exchange with Harry: he explains the betrayal, engages in a sharp debate about Harry using Expelliarmus, accuses Harry of near-suicidal recklessness, and Harry pushes back defiantly. This exchange ('the time for Disarming is past!'; 'I won't blast people out of my way just because they're there — that's Voldemort's job') is a defining moment of Lupin as mentor, moral interlocutor, and intellectual equal to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses this to a single line: 'We've been betrayed. Voldemort knew you were being moved tonight. I had to make sure you weren't an impostor.' The Expelliarmus debate, Lupin's 'painful restraint,' Harry's defiance, and the entire thematic exchange about signature moves and Voldemort's methods are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Expelliarmus debate is one of the most important mentor-student exchanges in the saga — it foreshadows the climax of Deathly Hallows (Harry using Expelliarmus against Voldemort) and establishes Lupin as someone who challenges Harry intellectually and morally, not just emotionally. Its absence removes Lupin's function as a wise, probing mentor and severs a key thematic thread.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Burrow yard, Lupin's suspicion of Mundungus and 'like James' exchange
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lupin drain his glass and ask pointedly 'So Mundungus disappeared?' — creating a tense atmosphere where everyone watches him. This leads to the exchange where Lupin looks at Harry with a pitying expression and says 'I think you're like James — who would have regarded it as the height of dishonor to mistrust his friends,' a line that cuts Harry deeply by invoking his father's fatal flaw. Lupin then pivots immediately to action ('There's work to do') and leaves with Bill to recover Mad-Eye's body.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange is entirely absent from the film corpus. The toast to Mad-Eye and Lupin's 'Understood' line replace this material. The 'like James' comparison and the recovery of Mad-Eye's body mission do not appear.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'like James' line is one of Lupin's most layered moments — it simultaneously honours and warns Harry, invoking Pettigrew's betrayal without naming it, and shows Lupin's unique insight into the Potter legacy. Its absence reduces Lupin from someone who actively shapes Harry's self-understanding to a background witness.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Grimmauld Place, Lupin's offer to join the trio and the confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Grimmauld Place scene is one of Lupin's defining moments across the entire saga: he arrives, briefs the trio on the political situation at length and with authority, then makes his offer to join them, reveals Tonks's pregnancy with a 'grimace,' confesses his self-loathing ('I made a grave mistake in marrying Tonks'), and is finally confronted by Harry who calls him a coward. Lupin draws his wand, blasts Harry, and leaves. This scene establishes Lupin's internal conflict about his werewolf condition, his near-abandonment of responsibility, and Harry's moral courage in confronting his father's friend.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear anywhere in the film corpus. There is no Grimmauld Place briefing scene with Lupin, no offer to join the trio, no revelation of the pregnancy in this context, no cowardice confrontation, and no wand-blast exit.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging omission for Lupin's character arc. It removes his central internal conflict (shame about his condition leading to near-abandonment of wife and unborn child), his most morally complex moment, Harry's role in forcing him back to his responsibilities, and the entire arc of Lupin's redemption that culminates in his joyful announcement of Teddy's birth. Without this scene, Lupin's arc from flawed self-loathing man to redeemed father is invisible to film audiences. It also strips Harry of a crucial moment of moral agency and growth.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Wedding, Lupin's unhappy demeanour and departure
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes at the birthday dinner that Lupin 'smiled as he shook Harry's hand' but 'looked rather unhappy,' while Tonks 'looked simply radiant' — a clear signal of marital tension. At the wedding, Lupin gives Harry 'a swift smile' but his 'face fell again into lines of misery.' This visible unhappiness is the book's way of signalling the unresolved Grimmauld Place conflict to come.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's wedding scene (Film Corpus Scene 7) shows Lupin standing behind Harry, 'staring at Tonks with affection,' then grinning and clapping Harry on the shoulder after asking him to be godfather. He 'hikes off into the darkness' to stand guard. There is no visible unhappiness, no marital tension signalled.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without the Grimmauld Place confrontation scene (which is also absent from the film), the wedding's signals of Lupin's unhappiness have nowhere to resolve. But within the wedding scene itself, replacing visible misery with warmth and affection removes the only available hint that something is wrong in the Lupin marriage — flattening the character and losing the dramatic texture the book carefully builds.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Wedding, godfather offer timing
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin asks Harry to be godfather at Shell Cottage — after Teddy is born, in a scene of overwhelming joy, having returned from the Grimmauld Place confrontation and reconciled with Tonks. The offer is earned by the full arc of Lupin's redemption.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 7) moves the godfather offer to the wedding, delivered as a whispered aside. Tonks is shown with 'hand to her belly' and the offer is made before any of the crisis or resolution of the Grimmauld Place arc. Lupin 'grins, claps Harry on the shoulder' and moves on.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Relocating the godfather offer to the wedding collapses the emotional arc entirely. In the book, the offer carries the weight of Lupin's full redemption journey — he has faced his cowardice, returned to Tonks, and now joyfully embraces fatherhood and asks Harry to share in it. As a wedding-scene aside it becomes a pleasant moment without dramatic resonance, and it cannot carry its true meaning since the Grimmauld Place scene that motivates it does not exist in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 1 - Seven Potters aftermath, Tonks's return and Lupin's barely-controlled fear
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes: 'Remus!' Tonks cried as she staggered off the broom into Lupin's arms. His face was set and white: He seemed unable to speak.' After she explains what happened, 'A muscle was jumping in Lupin's jaw. He nodded, but seemed unable to say anything else.' When she finishes, 'Lupin sounded almost angry at Tonks' asking what kept her. This is a precise portrait of a man containing terror for his wife through a veneer of controlled anger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 5) shows Tonks arriving and saying Ron 'Deserves that. Brilliant, he was.' The reunion with Lupin is minimal — there is no equivalent of the jaw-muscle, the white face, the barely-suppressed emotion. Lupin's line in the film is the institutional 'Understood' in response to Harry's trust speech.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's precise physical detail — set white face, jumping jaw muscle, near-inability to speak — conveys the depth of Lupin's feeling for Tonks without sentimentality. This is the primary film opportunity to establish their relationship as emotionally real and high-stakes. Its absence means the Lupin-Tonks relationship has almost no emotional texture in the films, making their deaths later carry less weight.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Battle of Hogwarts, Lupin's original quote and leadership
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book has Lupin arrive at the Room of Requirement, meet Harry at the foot of the stairs ('Harry, what's happening?'), participate in the battle briefing where Kingsley identifies 'Remus' as leading a ground group, mediate in the Weasley family tension (suggesting Ginny stay in the Room of Requirement), and show the photograph of Teddy. These are all small but accumulating acts of leadership, warmth, and family feeling.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 11) gives Lupin an invented line — 'It's the quality of one's conviction that determines success, not the number of one's followers' — which he attributes to himself ('Me.') with a knowing smile. This is not present in the book corpus and replaces the quieter, functional characterisation of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Lupin at the Battle of Hogwarts is purposeful and warm but not aphoristic. The invented quote gives him a cinematic 'cool professor' register — detached, slightly ironic, quotable — that is foreign to the character as written. The book's Lupin leads through action and care, not through bon mots. This reframes his personality toward a different archetype.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Great Hall, Lupin and Tonks's bodies
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book describes Harry seeing 'Remus and Tonks, pale and still and peaceful-looking, apparently asleep beneath the dark, enchanted ceiling,' then 'He turned away and ran up the marble staircase. Lupin, Tonks… He yearned not to feel… He wished he could rip out his heart, his innards, everything that was screaming inside him.' Later: 'the pain of losing Fred and Lupin and Tonks pierced him like a physical wound every few steps.' The Forest scene has Harry address Lupin specifically: 'right after you'd had your son... Remus, I'm sorry' and Lupin replies about dying to make a world his son could live in.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 14) shows Lupin and Tonks with 'their blood-stained fingers clumsily intertwined' — a visual addition not in the book. Harry's internal monologue about Lupin is absent. In the Forest scene (Scene 15), Lupin's line is reduced to 'Others will tell him what his mother and father died for. Someday he'll understand.' The specific apology from Harry ('right after you'd had your son') and Lupin's articulated motivation ('I was trying to make a world in which he could live a happier life') are cut or compressed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lupin's spoken motivation in the Forest — 'I was trying to make a world in which he could live a happier life' — is the culminating statement of his arc: the man who nearly abandoned his child instead died to protect all children, including his own. Reducing this to 'others will tell him' removes the thematic closure of Lupin's entire DH journey. The intertwined fingers are a compensatory visual gesture that cannot carry the same meaning as the spoken arc resolution.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Tonks's arrival at the Battle (cut scene per NON-THEATRICAL exclusion)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that Tonks left Teddy with her mother specifically to fight beside Lupin ('I couldn't stand not knowing... She'll look after him'). This is a parallel act to Lupin's own choice — both parents chose the fight, and both died together. Aberforth's line 'He was dueling Dolohov, haven't seen him since' and Tonks's anguished search for Remus establish their separation and mutual fear before death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Per the non-theatrical exclusion instruction, the scene of Tonks arriving at the Battle and searching for Lupin was cut from the theatrical release. It appears in the film corpus (Scene 11) only as the non-excluded portion showing Lupin and Tonks reuniting on the battlements — but the book's searching, separation, and Aberforth's report are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The theatrical cut removes all of the book's dramatic separation of Lupin and Tonks during the battle — Tonks's frantic search, Aberforth's worried report, Ginny's reassurance. This means their deaths side by side have no preceding tension or earned tragedy in the film. They appear together in one scene and are next seen dead, with no dramatic arc between. The emotional impact of their simultaneous deaths is substantially reduced.
